A0224.title: Benign Crawler Whitelisting
A0224.definition: Identifying legitimate search-engine and compliant crawlers via IP allowlists, User-Agent recognition, and reverse DNS (rDNS) verification, then allowing them through — preventing anti-scraping policies from falsely blocking benign bots and causing SEO or indexing losses.
A0224.description: Anti-crawling measures, while blocking malicious crawlers, can easily cause collateral damage to legitimate search engine bots (e.g., Googlebot, Bingbot, Baidu Spider, Sogou Spider), resulting in pages not being indexed and a decline in organic search traffic. Benign crawler allowlisting uses a three-step verification process to identify legitimate crawlers: first, IP allowlisting, which checks whether the request's source IP falls within the officially published crawler IP ranges of search engines; second, User-Agent identification, matching the official crawler UA patterns; third, reverse DNS (rDNS) resolution, performing a reverse lookup on the request IP and verifying the forward-resolution loop to prevent attackers from forging a Googlebot UA to bypass detection. The combination of these three methods effectively distinguishes real search engine crawlers from malicious crawlers impersonating them. This approach complements proxy identification (A0038) and IP intelligence (A0016-001), serving as a prerequisite companion to the cloud-based anti-crawling (A0003) strategy—first allowing benign crawlers through, then applying identification and restrictions to the remaining traffic, thereby reducing the false positive rate.
A0224.limitation: Benign crawler allowlisting depends on the timely maintenance of official search engine IP ranges and rDNS data; if IP ranges change without synchronized updates, it may lead to false positives or missed blocks. Some compliant crawlers do not publish their IP ranges or use third-party CDN egress points, making them difficult to include in the allowlist. Attackers who can control rDNS records or use proxies within search engine IP ranges may still bypass the detection by impersonation, so this method cannot be used as a sole trust anchor and must rely on combined UA and IP verification.
